query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A minor addition of titanium (approximately 3–5 atomic %) into equal‐atomic NbMoTaW improves room-temperature ductility via a transformation-induced plasticity mechanism or by enabling extra slip systems, while retaining the high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance of the pure alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy NbMoTaW with excellent mechanical performance at 1600 °C but poor ductility at room temperature and irradiation resistance based on first-principles predictions.
generation.intervention: Introduce 3–5 at% Ti into the NbMoTaW alloy composition during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Testing at room temperature, at 1600 °C, and under controlled irradiation conditions representative of service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The Ti addition is proposed to promote nanoscale local ordering or controlled secondary phase formation at grain boundaries, which lowers the energy barrier for dislocation motion at room temperature without altering the overall high-temperature BCC structure.
generation.mechanism: Ti atoms are hypothesized to induce localized structural modifications (e.g., facilitating a transformation-induced plasticity response or activating additional slip systems) that enhance dislocation mobility at lower temperatures; meanwhile, at high temperatures the dominant BCC phase is retained and the irradiation tolerance remains governed by the overall chemical homogeneity and atomic-scale disorder.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under room temperature, the Ti-modified alloy will exhibit a significant improvement in ductility relative to the untreated NbMoTaW. At 1600 °C, it will maintain its high strength and structural integrity, and under irradiation, it will show comparable resistance to damage as the baseline alloy.
generation.baseline: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW alloy with its documented excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance, but poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only within a narrow Ti doping range (approximately 3–5 at%); higher Ti concentrations might lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases, compromising the high-temperature and irradiation performance.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is based on plausible modifications of dislocation activity by minor Ti additions, direct experimental evidence linking such microstructural changes to improved room-temperature ductility (without detrimental side effects) is currently lacking.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize samples of the baseline NbMoTaW alloy and variants with 3–5 at% Ti addition under identical processing conditions. Perform systematic mechanical testing at room temperature and at 1600 °C, and subject samples to controlled ion irradiation. Use advanced microscopy and diffraction techniques to evaluate microstructural changes.
measurements: Post-irradiation microstructural characterization (TEM/SEM, defect density analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility compared to the baseline, or if its high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance is compromised (e.g., observable brittle phase formation, increased defect accumulation), the hypothesis will be falsified.
